How to Remove Your Personal Data from Data Broker and People-Search Sites

By RMA — Web Reputation Agency

People-search sites, online directories and data brokers operating in Europe are bound by the GDPR, so you can require them to stop using and delete your data through erasure and objection requests. The work is methodical rather than complicated: find where your data appears, send a precise request to each site, escalate to the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali when ignored, and check periodically that nothing returns.

Where these sites get your data

Data brokers rarely invent information; they assemble it from many legitimate and less legitimate sources and combine it into a profile linked to your name. Knowing the source tells you where to act first, because removing a profile while its source remains open often means it reappears.

  • Public registers, such as company records and lists of professionals, which show roles, addresses of registered offices and sometimes tax codes.
  • Telephone directories and their online copies, which include anyone who agreed to be listed years ago.
  • Social networks, forums and review sites, scraped automatically for names, photos, employers and locations.
  • Marketing databases built from contests, loyalty cards and online forms, traded between companies.
  • Data leaked in security breaches, which circulates on low-quality aggregators.

In Italy the most frequent cases involve directory-style sites that republish phone numbers and home addresses, and aggregator pages that combine company register data with personal details of directors and sole traders.

What the GDPR allows you to demand

When a site processes your personal data without your consent, you have three key rights: to know what it holds, to object to the processing, and to obtain erasure. Together they are the legal basis to remove personal data from internet databases run by companies.

Access and transparency

Art. 15 GDPR gives you the right to a copy of your data and to know its source, purposes and recipients. Art. 14 already obliges a company that collected data from third parties to inform you, which most brokers fail to do; this omission is itself a useful argument in a later complaint.

Objection and erasure

Under art. 21 you can object to processing based on legitimate interest, and the company must stop unless it demonstrates compelling grounds that override your interests. Objection to direct marketing is absolute. Art. 17 then requires erasure when data is no longer necessary, consent has been withdrawn, an objection has been upheld or the processing is unlawful. The controller must reply within one month, extendable by two further months for complex requests, and must tell you if it refuses and why.

How to send an effective request

A short, specific request sent to the right address works far better than a generic complaint. Most sites publish a privacy contact or a data protection officer (DPO) in their privacy policy.

  1. List the exact URLs and the data each shows: name, address, phone number, email, date of birth, photos.
  2. Write to the privacy contact citing arts. 15, 17 and 21 GDPR, asking for the source of the data, erasure and confirmation that it will not be processed again.
  3. Provide only the identification needed to match your record; never send a full copy of an ID document without masking non-essential fields.
  4. Keep proof of sending, such as PEC (certified email) for Italian companies or email with delivery receipt.
  5. Diary the one-month deadline and check the pages again once it expires.

Some sites offer an online opt-out form. Using it is usually faster, but take screenshots of the submission, because forms leave no record on your side.

Sites that ignore you or operate outside the EU

An unanswered request or a refusal without valid reasons is the trigger for a complaint (reclamo) to the Garante, which can order the controller to comply and impose sanctions. The complaint should attach your request, proof of sending and screenshots of the data still online.

Brokers based outside the European Union are not automatically out of reach. Under art. 3(2) GDPR, the regulation applies to companies that offer services to people in the EU or monitor their behaviour, and such companies should appoint a representative in the EU under art. 27. When neither the operator nor a representative can be identified, the hosting provider can receive a notice under the Digital Services Act, and Google can be asked to drop the pages from results on privacy grounds. Our article on what the right to be forgotten can remove from Google explains where that route ends.

Deleting data at the broker solves the cause; removing it from Google only hides the symptom. Where possible, do both, in that order.

DIY or a personal data removal service

A personal data removal service saves time when your data appears on many sites, but it cannot exercise rights that you do not have, and it needs your mandate to act on your behalf. The choice depends on the number of sources and on how sensitive your situation is.

AspectDoing it yourselfUsing a service
Best forA handful of known sitesDozens of sites, recurring reappearance, public exposure
CoverageOnly the sites you findSystematic searches across directories and aggregators
Follow-upManual checks and remindersScheduled re-checks and escalation to the Garante or hosts
Risk to watchMissing deadlinesSharing more data with the provider than necessary

Many automated services focus on American people-search sites and cover European and Italian sources only partially, so ask for the list of sites included before signing. The difference between deleting content at the source and making it harder to find is explained in our comparison of removal, deindexing and suppression.

Keeping your data off the internet

To delete personal information online for good, you also need to close the channels that feed brokers in the first place. Prevention is what turns a one-off clean-up into a lasting result.

Ask your telephone operator not to list your number in public directories, and register landline and mobile numbers in the Registro pubblico delle opposizioni to object to telemarketing use. Review privacy settings on social networks so that employer, city and contacts are not public, and avoid giving your main phone number and email to contests or loyalty schemes. Repeat a search for your name, phone number and address every few months, because new aggregators appear regularly.
